topic: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
title: Deprivation of liberty, DoLS and the LPS position
blurb: Choose the right legal route when care for a person with a learning disability deprives them of liberty, and know what is and is not in force.
question: Callum, 26, has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about his care. He has moved into a care home, and the team has concluded that his care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. Which legal route authorises this?

teach.h: Liberty is a right, so restriction needs lawful authority
teach.body: Article 5 of the Human Rights Act protects liberty. When a person who lacks capacity is cared for in a way that deprives them of liberty, that deprivation must be authorised by law. Best interests alone are not enough, and a relative cannot consent on the person's behalf. In plain English: if care takes away someone's freedom, there must be a legal process that checks it is necessary and gives the person a way to challenge it.
teach.cite: HRA 1998 Sch 1 Art 5; MCA 2005 s1(5)-(6), Sch A1

root.label:
Care amounts to a deprivation
of liberty; person lacks capacity

teach.caption: Many people with a learning disability live in supported living, so the Court of Protection route matters in this field.

steps.label: Identify
steps.sub: Team recognises a likely deprivation of liberty

steps.label: Request
steps.sub: Managing authority asks the local authority

steps.label: Urgent if needed
steps.sub: Home or hospital gives itself up to 7 days

steps.label: Assess
steps.sub: Local authority checks the qualifying requirements

teach.h: Scenario: Callum moves into a care home
teach.body: Callum, 26, has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about his care. The care home team agree his arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. The registered nurse makes sure the home, as managing authority, requests a standard authorisation from the local authority, and gives an urgent authorisation if the need is immediate. Meanwhile staff keep restrictions to the least needed, use his communication passport and involve his mother as someone to consult, not as someone who can consent for him.

teach.h: The legal test is under review
teach.body: Whether a particular set of arrangements amounts to a deprivation of liberty is a question the courts have recently revisited: a Supreme Court judgment in June 2026 is reported to have changed the approach, and the government is assessing what it means. Do not decide this alone from memory. Take the question to your trust's MCA or DoLS lead. What has not changed: restrictions must be in the person's best interests, necessary, proportionate and the least restrictive option.

teach.h: DoLS and LPS: what is live?
teach.caption: LPS were delayed in 2023. A consultation was promised for 2026; the government is still assessing the effect of the 2026 judgment.
MCA s1(6): is there a less restrictive way to achieve the same purpose?

items: A relevant person's representative keeps in contact and represents the person (Sch A1 para 139).
The person or representative can ask the Court of Protection to decide whether the qualifying requirements are met, how long the authorisation lasts and its conditions (MCA s21A).
Staff support the person to express objections; an objection is a signal to review and to help them challenge.
Record restrictions, reasons and reviews in the care plan.

teach.text: Parents and support workers cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for an adult. And DoLS does not reach supported living or 16 and 17 year olds: those go to the Court of Protection. LPS would have changed this, but LPS are not in force.

items: Deprivation of liberty of a person lacking capacity needs lawful authorisation (Article 5).
DoLS: hospitals and care homes, 18+; local authority grants; urgent 7 days (+7), standard up to 1 year.
Supported living, own home and ages 16-17: Court of Protection.
LPS are not implemented; DoLS is the live scheme.
Whether arrangements amount to a deprivation is under legal review: seek your MCA/DoLS lead's advice.

summary: You can now pick the correct authorisation route by setting and age, describe how DoLS works and how a person challenges it, and explain that LPS are not in force. You also know that the legal test for a deprivation of liberty is under review and when to seek specialist advice.

A.q: Callum, 26, has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about his care. He lives in a care home, and the team agrees his arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. Which route provides lawful authorisation?
options: Written agreement from his mother as next of kin
A Liberty Protection Safeguards authorisation
A DoLS authorisation from the local authority
A best interests decision made by his GP
A.why: In a care home, for a person aged 18 or over who lacks capacity, a deprivation of liberty is authorised under DoLS (MCA Schedule A1), granted by the local authority as supervisory body.

whyNot.0: A relative cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for an adult.
whyNot.1: The Liberty Protection Safeguards have not been implemented.
whyNot.3: A best interests decision does not by itself authorise a deprivation of liberty.

A.q: A nurse on a medical ward in England has requested a standard DoLS authorisation for Grace, 41, who has a learning disability. Which body grants the standard authorisation?
options: The hospital trust as managing authority
The local authority as supervisory body
The Care Quality Commission
The Office of the Public Guardian
A.why: MCA Sch A1 para 180: for hospitals in England the supervisory body is the local authority, which grants standard authorisations.

whyNot.0: The managing authority requests a standard authorisation and may give an urgent one, but does not grant the standard authorisation.
whyNot.2: The CQC monitors how DoLS is used but does not grant authorisations.
whyNot.3: The Office of the Public Guardian supervises deputies and registers attorneys; it does not grant DoLS.

A.q: In October 2026 a student nurse asks whether the Liberty Protection Safeguards have replaced DoLS for people with a learning disability. What is the correct reply?
options: Yes, LPS replaced DoLS in all settings in 2026
Yes, LPS now cover people in supported living
No, DoLS were replaced by Court of Protection orders
No, LPS are not implemented and DoLS remain in force
A.why: LPS (Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019) were delayed in 2023 and have not been implemented; DoLS remain the live scheme in hospitals and care homes.

whyNot.0: LPS have not come into force in any setting.
whyNot.1: LPS have not been brought in for supported living either; that route is the Court of Protection.
whyNot.2: The Court of Protection authorises deprivations outside hospitals and care homes; it has not replaced DoLS.

B.q: Arjun, 30, has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about his care. He has his own supported living tenancy, and the team agrees his care amounts to a deprivation of liberty. What is the correct route?
options: Apply to the Court of Protection for authorisation
Ask the local authority for a standard DoLS authorisation
Give an urgent DoLS authorisation for 7 days
Record a best interests decision in his support plan
B.why: DoLS cover hospitals and care homes only. A deprivation of liberty in supported living must be authorised by the Court of Protection.

whyNot.1: DoLS standard authorisations cannot be given for supported living.
whyNot.2: An urgent DoLS authorisation is given by a hospital or care home, not in supported living.
whyNot.3: A best interests record does not authorise a deprivation of liberty.

B.q: Katie, 17, has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about her care at a residential college. The team agrees the arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. Which route applies?
options: A DoLS authorisation from the local authority
Her parents' consent under parental responsibility
An application to the Court of Protection
A DoLS urgent authorisation by the college
B.why: DoLS apply from age 18 (Sch A1 para 13). For a 16 or 17 year old, a deprivation of liberty is authorised by the Court of Protection.

whyNot.1: Parents cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty of a 16 or 17 year old who lacks capacity; court authorisation is needed.
whyNot.3: A residential college is not a DoLS managing authority, and DoLS do not apply under 18.

B.q: A care home manager concludes that new arrangements for Bill, 54, who has a learning disability and lacks capacity, amount to a deprivation of liberty that must start today. How long can the home's urgent authorisation last before any extension?
options: Up to 72 hours
Up to 7 days
Up to 28 days
Up to 1 year
B.why: MCA Sch A1 para 78: an urgent authorisation given by the managing authority lasts up to 7 days, and it can be extended once, by the supervisory body, by up to 7 more days (paras 84-85).

whyNot.0: 72 hours is the length of some Mental Health Act holding powers, not a DoLS urgent authorisation.
whyNot.2: 28 days is the maximum for detention for assessment under section 2 of the Mental Health Act.
whyNot.3: Up to 1 year is the maximum for a standard authorisation.

C.q: Mo, 39, has a learning disability and lives in a care home under a standard DoLS authorisation. Using pictures and his own words he says every week that he wants to live with his sister. His representative is unsure what to do. What is the most appropriate action for the nurse?
options: Explain that the authorisation settles where he lives for a year
Ask his sister to agree that the home is in his best interests
Wait for the next review before recording his objection
Help his representative to bring a challenge to the court
C.why: MCA s21A lets the Court of Protection decide questions about a standard authorisation. A consistent objection should be recorded and the person and representative supported to challenge it.

whyNot.0: An authorisation can be reviewed and challenged at any time; it does not fix his home for a year.
whyNot.1: His sister's agreement does not deal with his objection or his right to challenge.
whyNot.2: His objection should be recorded now and acted on, not held for a later review.

C.q: Layla, 33, has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity about her care in a care home. Night staff propose locking her bedroom door from outside because she wanders at night. What should the registered nurse do first?
options: Lock the door and request a DoLS authorisation
Explore why she wanders and plan less restrictive support
Ask her parents to sign consent to the locked door
Lock the door for one week while staff observe her
C.why: MCA s1(6) and best interests: first look for the cause (pain, toilet needs, routine, sensory needs) and less restrictive options. Any restriction must be necessary, proportionate and recorded.

whyNot.0: Authorisation does not make an unnecessary restriction appropriate; less restrictive options come first.
whyNot.2: Parents cannot consent to restrictions on an adult's liberty.
whyNot.3: A trial of locking her in is still a restriction without first looking for a cause or less restrictive option.

C.q: After a court judgment in June 2026, a community team is unsure whether Theo's new support arrangements still amount to a deprivation of liberty. Theo, 45, has a learning disability and lacks capacity about his care. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Pause his support plan until the law is settled
Ask his brother to agree the plan in writing
Seek advice from the MCA and DoLS lead
Remove the restrictions until a court decides
C.why: The legal approach to identifying a deprivation of liberty is under review. The team should take specialist advice and follow current local guidance, while keeping care in his best interests and least restrictive.

whyNot.0: Stopping support could harm Theo; care continues while advice is sought.
whyNot.1: A relative's written agreement does not answer the legal question or authorise a deprivation.
whyNot.3: Removing all restrictions without assessment may expose Theo to serious risk.

reteach.title: Two questions: where, and how old?
reteach.question: Once the team agrees care amounts to a deprivation of liberty, how do you know which route to use?

blocks.h: Setting and age decide the route
blocks.body: Ask where the person lives and how old they are. Hospital or care home, 18 or over: DoLS, granted by the local authority. Anywhere else, such as supported living or the family home, or aged 16 or 17: the Court of Protection. Nobody else, not parents, not a GP, not a support worker, can authorise it.

blocks.text: LPS would have covered all settings from 16, but LPS are not in force. Teach and practise DoLS plus the Court of Protection.

explain.body: Article 5 protects liberty. A deprivation of liberty of someone lacking capacity needs a legal process with checks and a right to challenge. Best interests and family agreement are not enough.

test.q: Jo's father says he is happy to consent to the locked doors in the care home where Jo, 28, who lacks capacity, now lives. The team agrees the arrangements deprive her of liberty. What is the correct response?
options: His consent is valid because he is her nearest relative
His consent cannot authorise it; DoLS authorisation is needed
His consent is valid if it is written in her care plan
His consent is valid for 28 days until a review is held
test.why: A relative cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for an adult. In a care home, DoLS authorisation is needed.

whyNot.0: Being a close relative gives no power to consent to an adult's deprivation of liberty.
whyNot.2: Recording his view in the care plan does not make it a lawful authorisation.
whyNot.3: There is no 28-day consent period; authorisation is needed from the start.

explain.body: DoLS covers hospitals and care homes for people aged 18 or over. Supported living, the person's own home and 16 and 17 year olds go to the Court of Protection.

test.q: Which person's deprivation of liberty can be authorised under DoLS?
options: Ben, 17, in a residential special school
Sara, 35, in her own supported living flat
Ali, 52, on an acute hospital ward
Kim, 40, living in her parents' home
test.why: DoLS apply to people aged 18 or over in hospitals and care homes.

whyNot.1: Supported living is outside DoLS; the Court of Protection authorises it.
whyNot.3: A family home is outside DoLS; the Court of Protection authorises it.

explain.body: Urgent authorisation by the hospital or home: up to 7 days, extendable once by up to 7. Standard authorisation by the local authority: up to 1 year. A relevant person's representative is appointed, and s21A allows a challenge in the Court of Protection.

test.q: Who is appointed to keep in touch with and represent a person once a standard DoLS authorisation is given?
options: A relevant person's representative
The best interests assessor
The registered manager of the home
An independent mental health advocate
test.why: MCA Sch A1 para 139: the supervisory body appoints a relevant person's representative after a standard authorisation is given.

whyNot.1: The best interests assessor carries out an assessment; they are not the ongoing representative.
whyNot.2: The manager runs the managing authority and is not independent of the arrangement.
whyNot.3: IMHAs support patients under the Mental Health Act, not people under DoLS.

explain.body: DoLS is the live scheme. LPS, passed in 2019, are not implemented. The legal test for whether care amounts to a deprivation of liberty is under review after a June 2026 judgment, so seek specialist advice rather than deciding alone.

test.q: A care home nurse is updating a DoLS policy in October 2026. Which statement belongs in it?
options: LPS now apply to residents aged 16 and over
DoLS remain the scheme for authorising care here
Families can now authorise restrictions directly
Authorisations now come from the Court of Protection
test.why: DoLS (MCA Sch A1) remain in force for hospitals and care homes; LPS have not been implemented.

whyNot.2: Families cannot authorise a deprivation of liberty for an adult.
whyNot.3: Care home deprivations are authorised under DoLS by the local authority; the court hears challenges and covers other settings.
